prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: a near couch along the lower-left edge in frames 1–3 (roughly 0.3–0.8 m), a chair and backpack to the right at about 1–2 m, a freestanding sign ahead at about 3–5 m, and glass walls and corridor surfaces extending farther away. It makes the couch, chair, backpack, and the partial round tabletop at the bottom of frame 4 stand out from the floor, while the sign remains consistently farther in front; the chair and backpack shift toward the right edge and partly leave view as the camera turns left across frames 4–5. The person visible through or beside the glass in frames 4–5 appears several metres away, roughly 4–7 m, but is not cleanly separated by the depth map, so their distance, facing direction, and motion are uncertain. Brightness gives strong relative near/far ordering that is harder to judge from RGB alone, but the map is not metrically calibrated, merges similarly distant surfaces, blurs boundaries, and assigns unreliable depth around reflective glass, thin structures, and cropped objects.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies a foreground couch, a backpack, a chair in frames 3–4, and a person in frame 5, clarifying which visible regions belong to distinct instances and when the backpack overlaps the chair. The couch is within about 0.3–0.8 m of the wearer and partly outside the lower-left or lower-right image boundary; the chair and backpack are about 1–2 m away on the right in frames 1–3, then move toward or beyond the right edge as the camera turns, while the person remains several metres ahead-left of them. In frame 5 the person mask is upright and narrow, but it does not provide enough body detail to determine facing direction or whether the person looks toward the wearer; no other person is segmented. The map reveals object boundaries and occlusion more clearly than RGB, especially the backpack lying in front of the chair, but it is unreliable where it labels the freestanding sign as a refrigerator, inconsistently omits the chair, misses most architectural surfaces and the table, and changes the couch mask substantially when it is cropped.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no body or hand keypoints, no facing direction, no gaze evidence, and no arm-reach relationships for either the wearer or the distant person. It therefore cannot show whether the person approaches, retreats, turns, or becomes occluded; the RGB only shows that a person appears in the glass-side corridor in frames 4–5, roughly 4–7 m away and well beyond the wearer's arm reach. No yellow body skeleton or magenta hand skeleton is visible, including for the camera wearer, so objects near the wearer—such as the couch at roughly 0.3–0.8 m and the chair or backpack at roughly 1–2 m—cannot be associated with any limb position. The blank output is unreliable as a spatial map and most likely reflects missed pose detections, severe distance or scale limitations, occlusion, or the absence of visible wearer limbs rather than evidence that no person is present.
